analysis.one_liner: Raises income tax rates to 45–49% on income over $1 million and taxes capital gains at those rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add new tax brackets starting at $1 million of taxable income, with rates rising from 45% to 49% on the very largest incomes. It would also take away the lower capital gains rate for taxpayers whose income reaches the 45% bracket, so investment income for the richest households would be taxed like salary. The bill does not say what the extra revenue would pay for; it was introduced in April 2013 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the direct beneficiaries would have been everyone else in the tax system, since the new revenue would come entirely from households with taxable income above $1 million — roughly the top sliver of filers. Any gain to ordinary people would depend on Congress later spending the revenue on programs or using it to reduce deficits, which the bill does not itself specify.

how_it_helps.text: Adds new brackets starting at $1 million of taxable income, with rates of 45% (over $1M), 46% (over $10M), 47% (over $20M), 48% (over $100M), and 49% (over $1 billion), while leaving rates at or below 39.6% for everyone under $1 million [S3].

For taxpayers whose income reaches the 45% bracket, the bill would tax net capital gains at those ordinary rates instead of the lower capital gains rate, shifting the tax burden for the wealthiest filers from investment income toward parity with wage income [S3].

All new revenue would come from households above $1 million in taxable income; the rate tables keep every bracket at or below $450,000 unchanged from current law, so no filer under $1 million would see a rate increase [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households with taxable income over $1 million — about the top 0.3% of filers — through higher marginal rates of 45–49%, and especially the very largest incomes, which would pay up to 49 cents of every additional dollar. The capital gains provision would fall hardest on wealthy investors whose income comes from investments rather than wages.

drawbacks.text: A top marginal rate of 49% would be among the highest in modern U.S. history; critics argue rates that high reduce incentives to invest, take risks, and report income, and encourage tax avoidance through shelters and deferral [S3].

The bill raises revenue but does not direct it anywhere — it neither funds a program nor mandates deficit reduction, so the benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on later congressional choices [S2].

The capital gains change only applies to filers already in the 45% bracket, so many high earners with large investment income just below that line would keep the preferential capital gains rate, limiting how much the bill narrows the gap between wage and investment taxation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill asks the very highest earners to pay substantially more and leaves everyone else's rates untouched, which is a clean, progressive design on its face. Its honest weakness is that it is only a rate change: it does not close loopholes, it does not say what the money buys, and the capital gains fix reaches only the very largest incomes. Still, the cost falls exclusively on a small group with the greatest ability to pay.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on April 25, 2013, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote; the bill died there when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Fairness in Taxation Act of 2013 in the House on April 25, 2013, joined by six original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no Republican did [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with taxable income above $1 million, who kept the then-current 39.6% top rate and the lower capital gains rate for the rest of the Congress.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 25, 2013 and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: 8 of 435 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all eight cosponsors were Democrats, including the six who joined at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Dave Camp, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 2013 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill expired in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporting members were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill died in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.industry: Households with taxable income over $1 million
industries.note: The bill's entire cost would fall on this group, up to a 49% marginal rate on the largest incomes. Their continued lower rates under current law are the public's forgone revenue.

industries.industry: Wealthy investors and investment managers (private equity, hedge funds)
industries.note: The bill would strip the preferential capital gains rate from filers in the 45% bracket, taxing their investment gains at ordinary income rates. The preference these managers keep is the difference between how wage income and investment income are taxed.
